what: Time and peak memory of bootstrap/measure/stdlib_sample.argx: a JSON object of N members written with stdlib.json, validated, its keys indexed in stdlib.ordered_map, and its values sorted and searched with stdlib.vector.
how: bootstrap/measure/run.sh target/linux/debug/argorixc <sizes>; gcc 12.2 -O2 on Debian bookworm (Docker, rust:1-slim-bookworm), GNU time. 'default' keeps the C1 limits (1,000,000 steps, 1 MiB per buffer); 'lifted' removes the step limit only.

after_json_sort.change: stdlib.json finds duplicate keys with a stable merge sort instead of pairwise comparison (PR #52); the rest of the workload is unchanged.
after_json_sort.reading: 16,000 members take 1.35 s instead of 3.25 s, and the default budget now covers 1,000 members instead of 600 to 800. What stays superlinear is stdlib.ordered_map.insert, which shifts sorted columns; it is the next cost to remove if the compiler needs larger maps.

findings: Memory is not the constraint: peak RSS stays near 2 MB at 16,000 members, and the largest buffer (the document, about 14 bytes per member) reaches the 1 MiB per-buffer ceiling only past roughly 70,000 members.

Time is quadratic: each doubling of N costs about 4.3 to 4.4 times more. Two known sources: stdlib.json rejects duplicate keys by comparing each key with every earlier one, and stdlib.ordered_map inserts into sorted columns by shifting. Both are correct and deterministic; neither scales to large documents.
The default step budget is a test budget: between 600 and 800 members fit. A compiler run must be given its own budget by the driver rather than rely on the default.
not_measured: A sample of the real compiler: no Argorix compiler exists yet (ESP-010 onward). This workload stands in for its manifest and IR handling.
